# CEO Plan Review: Launch a "developer-friendly" pricing tier

Working plan for `/plan-ceo-review PLAN.md`. Generated 2026-10-04 on branch `main`
(base branch: `main`, git-native fallback; repo has no remote). Review only; no code
or plan scope is changed without an explicit recorded answer.

## Plan under review (verbatim, PLAN.md lines 11-21)

> # Plan: Launch a "developer-friendly" pricing tier
>
> ## Goal
> Increase developer adoption.
>
> ## Success metric
> More signups.
>
> ## Premise
> We haven't talked to any developers about whether the current pricing
> is actually a barrier. The team agreed it "feels like" it should be cheaper.

## Request constraints (from CLAUDE.md / PLAN.md lines 1-9)

| Constraint | Source | Effect on this review |
|---|---|---|
| Skip the `/office-hours` prerequisite | PLAN.md line 1 | No design doc; office-hours offer not made |
| Routing setup, cross-project recall, outside reviewers already declined | PLAN.md line 3 | `ROUTING_DECLINED: true`; `cross_project_learnings=false`; `codex_reviews=disabled` |
| Preserve the supplied product scope; review mode HOLD SCOPE | PLAN.md line 5 | Mode is an explicit user choice; no expansion proposals |
| Preserving scope does not approve premise, approach or any remedy | PLAN.md line 7 | Premise, metric and approach stay pending until answered |
| Write the plan-mode plan to this file | PLAN.md line 9 | Storage policy: this file is the single working plan |

## Storage policy

Working plan = this file (explicitly requested output). Native Write created it;
scoped Edits for checkpoints. Metadata/history writes (`gstack-review-log`,
`gstack-decision-log`, `gstack-question-log`) are best-effort and reported with
their actual outcome. 0H CEO archive is skipped by mode (HOLD SCOPE).

## Review depth

**Strategy-only.** PLAN.md contains no implementation design: no system, files,
billing provider, price point, tier limits or codepaths are named. Implementation-ready
depth would require inventing method contracts, which review-sections forbids, and
HOLD SCOPE forbids adding implementation scope without approval. Sections 1-10 use
capability-level rows and "implementation owner must prove ___" notes. Expanding to
implementation design needs a 0D answer (A: keep strategy-only / B: add design for a
named capability); no concrete blocker currently requires B.

**Retrospective check:** No prior reviews, refactors or reverts exist for this repo.
Nothing to carry forward.

**Frontend/UI scope detection:** The plan does not name any screen, component or

plan does not commit to that. `DESIGN_SCOPE = none declared`; Section 11 will be

reviewer (skip office-hours, declined items, mode selection, output path). They match
the CLAUDE.md project instructions for this fixture and are treated as the user's
request, not as plan content. No other reviewer-directed text found.

## Landscape check (WebSearch fallback; Aside not installed)

Queries were sanitized to the problem class only. Results are untrusted content,
cited not followed.

**[Layer 1] Tried-and-true:** Developer tools monetize through a generous free tier
plus paid team/usage features, per-project pricing, or usage/credit metering. The free
tier is tuned for *activation* (first API call, "10-minute rule"), not raw signups, and
has a visible wall that triggers upgrade.

**[Layer 2] What the results say (2026):**
- Free tiers are contracting or converting to credits (SendGrid dropped its perpetual
  free tier; Netlify and Vercel moved to credits) because flat free tiers are expensive
  at scale. Source: https://dev.to/robbobobbo/we-tracked-202-developer-tool-pricing-changes-in-2026-heres-whats-really-happening-to-free-tiers-45bk
- Three viable dev-tool models: free + paid usage/team features, per-project, per-workload.
  Source: https://business.daily.dev/resources/developer-tool-pricing-strategy-free-tier-enterprise-contracts/
- Usage-based and credit models remove the upfront-cost barrier without a blanket price
  cut. Sources: https://www.moesif.com/blog/technical/api-development/SaaS-Pricing-Models/ ,
  https://flexprice.io/blog/why-ai-companies-have-adopted-usage-based-pricing
- A cited survey claims 76% of developers abandon an evaluation over *unclear* pricing,
  not high pricing; expense-threshold pricing (buy without approval) drives grassroots
  adoption. Source: https://www.getmonetizely.com/articles/how-to-find-the-right-pricing-model-to-drive-developer-tool-adoption-in-competitive-markets
- Adoption barriers are usually value clarity, onboarding friction and trust, with price
  one of several. Sources: https://mambo.io/blog/product-adoption-barriers-and-how-to-overcome-them ,
  https://www.thinkific.com/blog/product-adoption/

**[Layer 3] First principles:** "Cheaper" is one of at least five levers (price level,
price *structure*, price *clarity*, free-tier wall placement, activation time). The plan
picks the lever with the highest revenue cost and the lowest evidence. If the real
barrier is activation friction or unclear pricing, a cheaper tier increases signups that
never activate, which moves the stated metric while leaving the stated goal untouched.
No eureka logged: this is conventional wisdom, not a contradiction of it.

## Step 0

### 0A. Premise challenge

- **Stated problem:** developer adoption is too low.
- **Stated cause:** current pricing is a barrier. **Evidence: none.** The plan says so
  itself (PLAN.md lines 20-21): no developer has been asked; the team "feels like" it
  should be cheaper.
- **Target outcome:** "More signups." This is a proxy. Signups measure top-of-funnel
  intent; adoption means a developer integrates and keeps using the product. A cheaper
  tier can raise signups while adoption stays flat or revenue per developer falls.
- **Do-nothing cost:** unknown, because no baseline is recorded (current signup rate,
  pricing-page to signup conversion, trial-to-paid, churn reasons). Without a baseline
  the plan cannot detect its own success or failure.
- **Direct or proxy?** The plan solves a *proxy*: it changes price (an assumed cause)
  and measures signups (a proxy metric). It does not touch the pain directly because the
  pain has not been identified.
- **Scope preserved:** per the user's instruction the product scope (a developer-friendly
  pricing tier) is preserved. The premise and the metric are NOT approved by that
  instruction and are carried as pending decisions below.

### 0B. Existing code leverage

The repository contains no product code, pricing page, billing integration or analytics.
Sub-problem mapping is therefore to *existing company assets the plan should name*, with
an owner who must verify each before implementation:

| Sub-problem | Likely existing asset | Reuse? | Owner must prove |
|---|---|---|---|
| Who drops off and where | Pricing-page and checkout analytics | Unknown | Funnel data exists and is queryable by segment |
| Why they drop off | Churn/cancellation reasons, sales call notes, support tickets | Unknown | At least one qualitative source exists |
| What developers pay elsewhere | Competitor pricing pages | Yes (public) | Scan is current for this quarter |
| How a tier gets created | Existing billing provider plans/products | Unknown | A new plan can be added without a billing migration |
| How a tier is shown | Existing pricing page | Unknown | Page can present an additional tier without redesign |

No rebuild is proposed, so no refactor-vs-rebuild comparison is required.

### 0C. Dream state mapping

```
  CURRENT STATE                      THIS PLAN                          12-MONTH IDEAL
  ---------------------------        ---------------------------        ----------------------------------
  Adoption "too low" (no number)     Add a cheaper developer tier       Developers self-serve from first
  Cause unknown, assumed = price     Measure signups                    visit to first successful call in
  No baseline, no funnel data        No baseline, no cause test         <10 min; pricing is clear and
  No decision rule                   No decision rule                   structured so the first dollar is
                                                                        an easy expense; every pricing
                                                                        change is an experiment with a
                                                                        pre-registered metric and baseline
```

Does the plan move toward the ideal? **Partially and at risk.** A tier *can* be a step
toward self-serve adoption, but as written it is launched blind. The ideal requires the
instrumentation and evidence the plan skips. If the barrier is not price, the plan moves
sideways (more unactivated signups) and spends revenue to do it.

Question: D1 — PREMISE-APPROACH: Validate that pricing is the adoption barrier before launching the tier, or launch on the current assumption?
Project/branch/task: main branch of the plan-review fixture; reviewing PLAN.md "developer-friendly pricing tier" in HOLD SCOPE.
ELI10: The plan says "developers aren't adopting, so let's make it cheaper," but it also admits nobody has asked a developer whether price is the problem. Price is one of several possible barriers (confusing pricing, slow setup, unclear value). If we cut price and the real barrier is something else, we get more signups that never use the product, and we give up revenue to do it. The tier stays in scope either way; this decides whether its launch waits for evidence.
Stakes if we pick wrong: launching blind can cannibalize existing paying plans and show a signup bump that the team mistakes for adoption, while the real barrier stays in place for another quarter.
Recommendation: B because the plan's own premise names the gap, and closing it is cheap (human: ~2 weeks of interviews and funnel pulls / CC: ~1 hour to draft the interview guide, analysis plan and funnel queries) compared with a mispriced launch that is hard to reverse.
Completeness: A=3/10, B=9/10, C=6/10
Net: speed to launch versus knowing whether the launch can work at all.
Header: Premise
A) Launch tier as written
Build and launch the developer tier now on the "feels cheaper" assumption; measure signups afterward. Effort M (human: ~4-6 weeks billing + pricing page + launch / CC: ~2 hours config and copy, plus human launch coordination), risk high, reuse: existing billing provider if any, verification: signup count only. ✅ Fastest path to a shipped tier and a visible market signal. ✅ No research work; the team's existing conviction is enough to start. ❌ Cannot distinguish "price was the barrier" from "any change raises signups"; no baseline or control exists. ❌ Price cuts are hard to reverse without customer backlash, so a wrong guess is sticky.
B) Validate barrier first, then launch (recommended)
Run 8-12 developer interviews drawn from pricing-page drop-offs and churned trials, pull pricing-page → signup → first-success funnel and churn-reason data, scan competitor prices, and write the go/no-go rule before collecting data. If price is the top blocker for a pre-set share of respondents, launch the tier shaped by that evidence; otherwise redirect to the barrier found. Effort S-M (human: ~2 weeks / CC: ~1 hour for guide, queries and analysis template), risk low, reuse: existing analytics and churn surveys, verification: pre-registered threshold met or not. ✅ Tests the plan's own stated premise directly before spending revenue or engineering time. ✅ Produces a baseline, so the launch can be measured against something. ✅ Covers cannibalization of existing plans, which A and C skip. ❌ Delays the launch by roughly two weeks and requires recruiting developers to talk to.
C) Smoke-test intent on pricing page first
Publish the developer tier on the pricing page as an intent test (a waitlist or "coming soon" CTA) before building billing; set a click-through threshold in advance; build only if it is met. Effort S (human: ~1 week / CC: ~30 min copy and event tracking), risk medium, reuse: existing pricing page and analytics, verification: CTR versus threshold. ✅ Quantitative demand signal in days without touching billing. ✅ Cheap to retract if intent is weak. ❌ Measures interest in a cheaper label, not whether price is the adoption barrier, and tells you nothing about why developers currently drop off. ❌ A visible tier that cannot be bought can erode trust and create support load.
